Wiktionary’s coverage of Ansus terms (strong form) enPR: ănd, ĕnd IPA(key): /ænd/, /ɛnd/ (Received Pronunciation, General Australian, stressed form) IPA(key): [ænd] (Standard Southern British, stressed form) IPA(key): [and] (US, stressed form) IPA(key): [eənd], [ɛənd] (Canada, stressed form) IPA(key): [ɛənd], [æ(ː)nd] (Ireland, stressed form) IPA(key): /and/ (Dublin, stressed form) IPA(key): /æn/, /ænt/ (weak form) enPR: ən(d) IPA(key): /ənd/, /ən/, /æn/, /ɛn/, /ɛnd/, /n̩d/, /n̩/ Rhymes: -ænd, -ɛnd Homophones: an (unstressed), ant (in some accents), end (in some accents), in (unstressed) Inherited from Middle English and, an, from Old English and, ond, end, from Proto-West Germanic *andi, from Proto-Germanic *andi, *anþi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti (“facing opposite, near, in front of, before”). Cognate with Scots an (“and”), North Frisian än (“and”), Saterland Frisian un (“and”), West Frisian en (“and”), Dutch en, ende (“and”), German und (“and”), German Low German on, un (“and”), Luxembourgish an (“and”), Vilamovian an, ana (“and”), Yiddish און (un), אונ (un), אונד (und), אונ׳ (un', “and”), Danish end (“still; ever; even”), Faroese enn (“still, yet”), Icelandic en (“and”), enn (“still, yet”), Norwegian Bokmål enn (“and”), Norwegian Nynorsk en, enn (“and”), Swedish än (“still, yet”), Albanian edhe (“and”) (dialectal ênde, ênne), ende (“still, yet, therefore”), Latin ante (“opposite, in front of”), Ancient Greek ἀντί (antí, “opposite, facing”). Doublet of an ("if"). an' 'n' (n) and As a coordinating conjunction; expressing two elements to be taken together or in addition to each other. Used simply to connect two noun phrases, adjectives or adverbs. [from 8th c.] quotations ▼ Simply connecting two clauses or sentences. [from 8th c.] quotations ▼ Introducing a clause or sentence which follows on in time or consequence from the first. [from 9th c.] quotations ▼I'd been walking since sunrise, and I was hungry. (obsolete) Yet; but. [10th–17th c.] quotations ▼ Used to connect certain numbers: connecting units when they precede tens (now dated); connecting shillings to pence in a monetary quantity (now historical); connecting tens and units to hundreds, thousands etc. (now often omitted in US); to connect fractions to wholes. [from 10th c.] quotations ▼ (now colloquial or literary) Used to connect more than two elements together in a chain, sometimes to stress the number of elements. quotations ▼ Connecting two identical elements, with implications of continued or infinite repetition. [from 10th c.] quotations ▼ Introducing a parenthetical or explanatory clause. [from 10th c.] quotations ▼ Introducing the continuation of narration from a previous understood point; also used alone as a question: ‘and so what?’. quotations ▼ (now dialectal or somewhat colloquial) Used to connect two verbs where the second is dependent on the first: ‘to’. Used especially after come, go and try. [from 14th c.] quotations ▼ Introducing a qualitative difference between things having the same name; "as well as other". [from 16th c.] quotations ▼ Used to combine numbers in addition; plus (with singular or plural verb). [from 17th c.] quotations ▼Two and two is/are four. (heading) Expressing a condition. (now US dialect) If; provided that. [from 13th c.] quotations ▼ (obsolete) As if, as though. [15th–17th c.] quotations ▼ (mathematics, logic) Connecting two well-formed formulas to create a new well-formed formula that requires it to only be true when both of the two formulas are true. Inherited from Middle English ande, from Old English anda (“grudge, enmity, malice, envy, hatred, anger, zeal, annoyance, vexation; zeal; injury, mischief; fear, horror”) and Old Norse andi (“breath, wind, spirit”); both from Proto-Germanic *anadô (“breath, anger, zeal”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”). Cognate with German Ahnd, And (“woe, grief”), Danish ånde (“breath”), Swedish anda, ande (“spirit, breath, wind, ingenuity, intellect”), Icelandic andi (“spirit”), Albanian ëndë (“pleasure, delight”), Latin animus (“spirit, soul”). Related to onde. aynd, eynd and (plural ands) (UK dialectal) Breath. (UK dialectal) Sea smoke; steam fog. Inherited from Middle English anden, from Old English andian (“to be envious or jealous, envy”) and Old Norse anda (“to breathe”); both from Proto-Germanic *anadōną (“to breathe, sputter”). Cognate with German ahnden (“to avenge, punish”), Danish ånde (“to breathe”), Swedish andas (“to breathe”), Icelandic anda (“to breathe”). See above. eind, eynd, ein and (third-person singular simple present ands, present participle anding, simple past and past participle anded) (UK dialectal, intransitive) To breathe; whisper; devise; imagine. -dan, ADN, DAN, DNA, Dan, Dan., NAD, NDA, dan, dna, nad From Proto-Turkic *ānt (“oath”).[1] Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰦 (nt), Turkish ant.
